title: Decision Trees & Random Forests
subtitle: How a tree asks questions, why it memorizes, and how averaging hundreds of decorrelated trees turns a fragile model into the most reliable workhorse in tabular ML

objectives.title: Grow and Read a Decision Tree
objectives.description: Gini impurity in plain English, greedy binary splits, and plot_tree — a model you can print on one page and hand to a manager.

objectives.title: See Overfitting in a Tree
objectives.description: An unlimited tree reaches 99% training accuracy by carving a leaf for every quirky booking. max_depth and min_samples_leaf are its regularization knobs.

objectives.title: Build a Random Forest and Explain Why It Works
objectives.description: Bootstrap rows, sample features at every split, average the votes. Decorrelated trees cancel each other's errors — variance reduction you can watch happen.

objectives.title: Measure Importance Honestly
objectives.description: Impurity importance is biased toward high-cardinality columns; permutation importance on held-out data is not. Partial dependence shows the shape of the effect.

objectives.title: Bridge to Neural Networks
objectives.description: A tree asks about one clue with a hard yes/no; a neuron asks about a weighted mix with a soft answer. Overfitting, brakes and crowds (dropout) carry over — and on tables, tree ensembles still usually win.

agenda.title: Competition Check-In & Meet the Data: Hotel Bookings
agenda.description: Where every team stands on the leaderboard, then tonight's data: the competition's 83,573 training bookings from a city hotel and a resort hotel in Portugal, 37% canceled, 32 columns. Three of them are leaks. A one-line crosstab shows reservation_status is the target in disguise: every Check-Out stayed, every Canceled or No-Show canceled, no exceptions.
bulletPoints: reservation_status and reservation_status_date are the outcome in disguise: drop them or your leaderboard score is fiction
assigned_room_type is set at check-in. The test for every column: would I know this at the moment I predict?

agenda.title: How a Tree Asks Questions
agenda.description: 'Non-refundable deposit?' 'Booked more than two weeks ahead?' 'Canceled before?' A tree is a flowchart learned from data: at each node it auditions every clue and cut point and keeps the question that most reduces impurity. Gini = the chance that two random guests from the box disagree on cancellation.
bulletPoints: Greedy: the best split now, not the best tree overall
The manager's tree: six readable clues, three questions deep, the whole cancellation story on one screen (99% of non-refundable bookings cancel; 9% of bookings made a week or less ahead)

agenda.title: Watching a Tree Overfit
agenda.description: Depth 2 → 4 → 10 → unlimited on 28 columns. Training AUC climbs to a perfect 1.00 (99.7% accuracy) with 2,938 leaves for 24,000 bookings; test AUC peaks at 0.91 around depth 10 and falls to 0.81. The tree has memorized the training bookings. A validation curve over max_depth makes the sweet spot visible.
bulletPoints: Trees need no scaling and no one-hot — but a single tree is high-variance: two trees grown on two random halves of the same data disagree on 21% of test bookings
min_samples_leaf=50 beats every max_depth here (0.916 with 274 leaves): a manager would never write a policy based on one guest

agenda.title: From One Tree to a Forest
agenda.description: Galton's ox (1906): 787 guesses, the middle one within 1% of the truth. Bagging: grow many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, and average their votes — variance drops. Random forest adds the twist: at every split, only a random handful of features is eligible, so the trees make different mistakes. Out-of-bag score: a free validation set built from the rows each tree never saw.
bulletPoints: Adding trees never hurts: 5 trees already beat the best single tree, and the curve is flat after about 100
Hotel bookings (30k slice): best single tree 0.916 AUC, random forest 0.942 with no tuning, out-of-bag 0.939; two forests on two random halves disagree on only 4% of bookings

agenda.title: Which Features Matter — and the Bridge to Neural Networks
agenda.description: feature_importances_ (impurity) vs. permutation_importance on the test set — and the zero-signal trap: a pure-noise column and a made-up booking-ID column land 10th and 11th of 30 by impurity, ahead of real signals like parking spaces and customer type, and in the bottom three by permutation. Then partial dependence: how cancellation probability actually moves with lead time, special requests and past cancellations. Then the bridge: a tree asks about one clue, a neuron about a weighted mix; the same two clues drawn three ways (rectangles, a patchwork, curves); and why, on tables, the forest still beats a neural network.
bulletPoints: Permutation importance answers 'if I scrambled this column, how much would the model get worse?' — the honest question
Partial dependence for lead_time rises steeply over the first month (22% → 39%) and then creeps to about 48% at 300 days: the danger zone starts early
Neural network on the hotel table: 0.86 AUC without scaling, 0.93 with the full prep station, vs. 0.94 for the forest with none — as Grinsztajn et al. (NeurIPS 2022) found across 45 datasets

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Competition Check-In
agenda.description: Every team should have a leak-free pipeline and a forest submission by tonight: one cell swapped in the Competition Starter takes 5-fold AUC from about 0.89 to about 0.95. Next week, gradient boosting — the model that will probably win — and the tabular foundation models that might beat it.
bulletPoints: Project Milestone 1 (your problem and dataset, one paragraph) is due tonight, 11:59 PM
Leaderboard closes Mon Nov 9, 4:30 PM — upload the same predictions file on Canvas by then; the memo is due that night at 11:59 PM

activities.title: One Tree, Then Five Hundred: Predicting Hotel Cancellations
activities.description: Predict which bookings will cancel. Fit a single tree at several depths to watch overfitting, then a random forest, then ask the forest which features matter — twice, and notice the two answers disagree.

steps.title: Drop the leaks
steps.description: reservation_status, reservation_status_date, and (defensibly) assigned_room_type. Encode categoricals with OrdinalEncoder — trees don't need one-hot.

steps.title: Validation curve over depth
steps.description: DecisionTreeClassifier at max_depth 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, None. Train vs. test AUC. Find the peak and the gap.

steps.title: Grow the forest
steps.description: RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1). Compare oob_score_ with the test score.

steps.title: Two importances
steps.description: feature_importances_ vs. permutation_importance on the test set. Add a random noise column first and watch where each method ranks it.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/hotel_bookings.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url).sample(30_000, random_state=835)          # subsample for speed in class
leaks = ['reservation_status', 'reservation_status_date', 'assigned_room_type']
X = df.drop(columns=['is_canceled'] + leaks)
text = X.select_dtypes(exclude='number').columns
X[text] = X[text].apply(lambda c: c.astype('category').cat.codes)   # trees: code numbers are fine, no one-hot
X = X.fillna(-1)
X['noise'] = np.random.default_rng(835).normal(size=len(X))       # a column with zero signal
y = df['is_canceled']
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=835)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1, random_state=835)
rf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f'out-of-bag AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_tr, rf.oob_decision_function_[:, 1]):.3f}   test AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_te, rf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]):.3f}')

imp = pd.DataFrame({'impurity': rf.feature_importances_}, index=X.columns)
imp['permutation'] = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, scoring='roc_auc', n_repeats=5, random_state=835, n_jobs=-1).importances_mean
print(imp.sort_values('permutation', ascending=False).head(8).round(4))
print('noise column rank by impurity:', int((imp['impurity'] > imp.loc['noise', 'impurity']).sum()) + 1, 'of', len(imp))

activities.discussionNote: The forest reaches an AUC around 0.94 on a 30k-row slice with no tuning and no scaling — that is why it is the first serious model most practitioners reach for. But look at the importance table: country, deposit_type, market_segment, total_of_special_requests and lead_time lead by permutation, while the pure-noise column sits in the top third by impurity, ahead of real signals like parking spaces. Impurity importance rewards columns that offer many split points, not columns that predict. If you report feature importance to a manager, report the permutation version.

takeaways.text: A decision tree is a flowchart learned greedily from data: interpretable, scale-free, and high-variance. Depth and min_samples_leaf are its brakes; a single tree rarely ships.
A random forest is variance reduction by averaging decorrelated trees — bootstrap rows, sample features at every split. Hard to overfit by adding trees; the out-of-bag score is a free validation set.
Impurity importance lies about high-cardinality columns; permutation importance on held-out data does not. Partial dependence shows the shape of an effect, which is what a manager actually asks for.
